source.title: Scaling Behavior Foundation Model for Humanoid Robots
source.authors: Wei-Shuai Zeng; Kang-Ning Yin; Xiao-Jie Niu; Shun-Lin Lu; Weixiang Zhong; Jiahe Chen; Fei-Yu Jia; Xiao Chen; Zi-Rui Wang; Furui Xu; Ming Zhou; Kailin Li; Wei-Nan Zhang; He Wang; Li Yi; Da-Hua Lin; Jiang-Miao Pang; Jing-Bo Wang

record.file_problem: Whole paper and appendices are present. Many plotted values in the supplied text are garbled, so only the authors’ explicit qualitative descriptions of those results are extractable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses scaling and cites language-model scaling work, but its experiments measure humanoid-control performance rather than testing language-model held-out cross-entropy laws or their versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports scaling experiments on humanoid behavior foundation models, using tracking success rates and errors. These are not held-out language-model cross-entropy or tests of the power-law form; the explicit qualitative findings are recorded as related results under fits_no_version. The paper’s cited language-model scaling work is not itself a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The paper studies scaling of humanoid motion-tracking controllers trained with PPO. It measures tracking success rates and errors, not held-out language-model loss. It fits no power law and makes no extrapolation, allocation or exponent comparison. Kaplan et al. is cited only as inspiration, alongside a remark that this scaling study is limited compared with LLM studies. Even for V5, no power-law form is tested: results are qualitative trends such as diminishing returns, mode-dependent saturation and test-set-dependent gains.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that effective BFM scaling comes from coordinating three things: global-frame motion tracking, the balance between on-policy rollout quantity and reference-motion diversity, and the Humanoid Transformer architecture. They report large MPKPE reductions over existing controllers (over 10% local, 82% global). They acknowledge diminishing returns, mode-dependent saturation, and a scaling study limited compared with LLM studies.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses PPO motion tracking to train humanoid controllers and evaluates tracking performance; it does not use the language-model loss measurement or fitting recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with the balance of on-policy collection width and depth, whether added reference motions expand behavioral coverage, the test-set source, the control mode, and model architecture and capacity.

fits_no_version.finding: Jointly scaling parallel GPUs and rollout horizon (32 to 64) improved tracking performance. Scaling either alone gave no consistent trend.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In PPO-trained humanoid controllers, gains from more on-policy data depend on how width and depth of collection are balanced, not only on total quantity.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding in-domain reference motions (XXS to S) gave marginal gains. Adding heterogeneous sources (S to L) helped only on the cross-source test set.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of adding training motions to humanoid controllers depends on whether they expand behavioural coverage relevant to the evaluation set.

fits_no_version.finding: Transformer capacity scaling from 0.41M to 9.91M parameters gave diminishing returns, with some control modes saturating early.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gains from model capacity in humanoid behaviour foundation models diminish quickly and vary by control mode, within the small parameter range tested.

record.problems: The study explicitly says its scaling study is limited compared with large-language-model studies. The supplied plots are garbled, preventing extraction of their individual values; scaling results are mainly summarized qualitatively, and no uncertainty estimates are stated. The behavioral-coverage measure is acknowledged to depend on the dataset used to construct its clustering space.
record.rows_left_out: No readable individual plotted values could be extracted from Figures 4–9 or 12–29 in the supplied text. The rows therefore record only the authors’ explicit qualitative summaries, rather than separate model-by-mode metric values.

untested.parts: No held-out language-model pretraining loss and no power-law fit in parameters, data or compute.
No small-run fits extrapolated to larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and tokens.
The S/M/L/XL width-versus-depth sweep measures tracking metrics, not loss at fixed parameter count. Shape is also not held at fixed size.
Humanoid control is a different regime, but no power-law form is fitted or assessed for loss or performance.
No language-model downstream tasks and no link to pretraining loss.
No exponents, compute-optimal splits or fitting procedures are compared.

record.verdict_notes: Changed relation from 'discusses' to 'cites_only'. The language-model scaling-law papers are cited only as motivation, and no claim version is argued about. The plotted values are unreadable, so all rows are qualitative. No row bears on any version.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss or power-law relationship in parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run power-law fits or extrapolation to larger language-model runs are reported.
No fixed-compute language-model allocation between parameters and tokens is tested.
Architecture comparisons concern humanoid-control tracking performance, not held-out language-model loss at fixed parameter count.
The study scales humanoid models, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds for their loss or for other modalities and training regimes.
No language-model downstream-task performance or relationship to pretraining loss is measured.
The study does not fit or compare power-law exponents, compute-optimal splits, or fitting procedures.
